subject: Cloud Computing
title: Backup and Recovery Security
description: Learn Backup and Recovery Security in one minute.

hook.text: Ransomware encrypts your data and demands payment. If your backups are also encrypted, you're stuck.

buildup.text: Backups must be isolated from production. If an attacker reaches your backup, it's not a backup.

discovery.text: Immutable backups can't be modified or deleted, even by administrators. They survive ransomware attacks.

twist.text: Many companies discover their backup strategy is broken only during a real disaster. Testing is everything.

climax.text: Cloud makes backups easier than ever. But easier doesn't mean automatic — you still must design and test them.

punchline.text: Backups you never test aren't backups. They're hopes.

quiz.question: What are immutable backups?
options: Backups that cannot be modified or deleted, even by administrators
Backups stored in a different country than the original data
Backups that automatically update when the source data changes

details.summary: Backups are a critical security control, but they also create additional attack surfaces. Backups must be encrypted, access-controlled, stored in separate accounts, and regularly tested to ensure they can actually be restored when needed.
details.whyItMatters: Ransomware attackers specifically target backups to eliminate recovery options. Securing and testing backups is essential for resilience against destructive attacks.
takeaways: Encrypt backups and store them in separate accounts
Use immutable storage to prevent backup deletion
Test restore procedures regularly to verify recoverability

faq.question: What is immutable backup storage?
faq.answer: Immutable storage prevents backups from being deleted or modified for a defined retention period, even by administrators. This protects against ransomware and accidental deletion. AWS S3 Object Lock and Azure immutable blob storage provide this capability.

faq.question: How often should backup restores be tested?
faq.answer: Critical systems should have restore procedures tested quarterly at minimum. Many organizations discover during real incidents that their backups are corrupted, incomplete, or take far longer to restore than expected. Regular testing eliminates these dangerous surprises.
